name: Automation Bias
description: People can overweight automated recommendations and fail to adequately check them, even when the system is fallible. The result is both accepting wrong machine advice and missing problems the system failed to flag.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to AI copilots, recommender systems, moderation tools, fraud scoring, and decision-support UI: products need calibrated trust, inspectability, and verification cues so users neither blindly accept nor ignore automation.
prevalence_note: Rapidly becoming standard language in AI/HCI, clinical decision-support, and responsible-AI product discussions as teams design around over-reliance on model output.

findings.description: A systematic review of 74 papers found consistent evidence that people can over-rely on automated decision support, making both omission and commission errors when the aid is imperfect; trust, confidence, workload, task complexity, and time pressure all help mediate the effect, while accountability cues and interface design changes can mitigate it.
findings.source_title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
findings.source_venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

applications.title: Robert Williams' wrongful arrest: the first publicly reported facial-recognition automation-bias case
applications.description: In January 2020, Detroit police wrongfully arrested Robert Williams outside his home, in front of his family, based on a facial-recognition 'match' to a blurry surveillance still from a 2018 shoplifting incident. The match was incorrect -- Williams was not the person in the footage -- but officers relied on it to build a photo lineup and obtain an arrest warrant, omitting information that would have flagged the unreliability of both the facial-recognition result and the follow-up identification procedure. Williams was detained for 30 hours. The ACLU calls it the first publicly reported case of a false face-recognition match leading to a wrongful arrest; the resulting lawsuit against Detroit was settled in 2024.
applications.ethical_note: This is not a product-persuasion case but a real, severe, documented harm from automation bias in a high-stakes government system -- officers trusted an automated match over their own judgment and the plainly weak follow-up identification, with a real person's liberty as the cost. Graded manipulative_risk not because anyone was persuading Williams, but because the system's design (presenting an algorithmic match as reliable without disclosing its known error rates) actively misled the humans meant to check it.
